nodes.label: Ethics and regulation
nodes.question: What role does stakeholder involvement play in the success of conservation programs?
nodes.answer: Stakeholder involvement is perceived as closely related to the success of conservation programs, as it helps raise societal interest and awareness.
nodes.paragraph: Abstract In Europe, various conservation programs adopted to maintain or restore biodiversity have experienced differing levels ofsuccess. However, a synthesis about major factors for success of biodiversity-related conservation programs across ecosystems and national boundaries, such as incentives, subsidies, enforcement, participation, or spatial context, is missing. Using a balanced scorecard survey among experts, we analyzed and compared factors contributing to success or failure ofthree different conservation programs: two government programs (Natura 2000 and the ecological measures of the Water Framework Directive) and one conservation program of a non-governmental organization (NGO; Rewilding Europe), all focusing on habitat and species conservation. The experts perceived the NGO program as more successful in achievingbiodiversity-related aims than governmental conservation legislation. Among the factors perceived to in uence the success of biodiversity conservation, several stood out: Biodiversity-damaging subsidies, external economic interests competing with conservation goals or policies con icting with biodiversity conservation were recognized as major factors for the lack of conservation success. Outreach to raise societal interest and awareness as well as stakeholder involvement were perceived as closely related to the success of programs.

nodes.label: Analysis
nodes.question: How have the emotional states related to ecological loss been described in academic literature?
nodes.answer: The emotional states associated with an awareness of ecological loss have been described as both complex and complicated, including feelings of being paralyzed, daunted, or numb.
nodes.paragraph: Human Ecology https://doi.org/10.1007/s10745-25-580-2 Introduction Climate change and biodiversity loss are impacting people on a global scale. Although the effects of environmental crises on emotions have been studied using other terms (e.g., emotional impacts of environmental issues), eco-anxiety and eco-grief have only recently been acknowledged in academic literature (Pihkala, 2022 ). There is no formally defined mental health disorder or diagnosis to describe the emotions that are associated with an awareness of ecological loss. However, these emotional states have been described as both complex and complicated (Menning, 2017 ; Sideris, 2020) ), including feeling paralyzed, daunted, or numb, and have been connected to acute and chronic mental illnesses (Bourque & Cunsolo, 2014 : Cunsolo & Ellis, 2018 ). We applied the concept of environmental observers as people who purposely observe the environment and environmental information as part of their work or role in society (e.g., Hupp et al., 2015 ; Jones et al., 2023 ). Examples of environmental observers include volunteers and employees of environmental organizations, individuals Melanie Zurba melanie.zurba@dal.ca 1 School for Resource and Environmental Studies (SRES), Dalhousie University, 6100 University Ave, PO BOX 15000, Halifax, NS B3H 4R2, Canada 2 Faculty of Health, Dalhousie University, 5968 College Street, Halifax, NS B3H 4R2, Canada 3 Department of Biology and Centre for Forest Interdisciplinary Research, The University of Winnipeg, 515 Portage Ave, Winnipeg, MB R3B 2E9, Canada 4 Division of Fine Arts, NSCAD University, 5163 Duke St, Halifax, NS B3J 3J6, Canada 5 College of Nursing, Rady Faculty of Health Sciences, University of Manitoba, 89 Curry Place, Winnipeg, MB R3T 2N2, Canada 6 Department of History, Marion McCain Arts and Social Sciences Building, Dalhousie University, Halifax, NS B3H 4R2, Canada 7 Faculty of Nursing, University of New Brunswick, 55 Lutz Street, Moncton, NB E1G 1M2, CanadaAbstract This research aimed to contribute to understanding emotional reactions to ecological change in environmental observers, who purposely observe the environment and environmental information as part of their work or role in society (e.g., citizen scientists, environmental professionals, Indigenous knowledge keepers).

nodes.id: Subtopic:Environment|Life on land|Community conservation|Conservation awareness programs_qna_002
nodes.label: Science and tech
nodes.question: What research approach was used in this subset of the study?
nodes.answer: A phenomenological approach was used to understand the experiences and learning of observers related to ecological loss.
nodes.paragraph: This research is part of a broader research project that aims to develop an enhanced understanding of how different groups in Canadian society speak about and process the emotions associated with climate change and other forms of ecological loss. The project focuses on the Boreal and Atlantic ecoregions, two ecozones experiencing considerable impacts from climate change (e.g., increased wildfire numbers and severity and increased storm severity). The authors/research team includes diverse positionalities and roles in research (i.e., senior researchers and graduate students) representing environmental studies, biology, history/Indigenous studies, fine arts, and nursing. This subset of the more extensive study used a phenomenological approach to understand how observers experiences and learning adjacent to ecological loss impacted their emotions, decisions, and actions relative to their roles connecting to the environment. Specifically, our objectives were to: 1) Examine how environmental observers learn about the changing environment (i.e., through communications and (or) direct observation); 2) Explore how such learning impacts the emotional reactions of environmental observers; 3) Develop a deeper understanding of how emotional aspects of learning might be changing the actions (e.g., decision-making and (or) direct forms of action) of environmental observers; and, 4) Gain insight into how actions triggered by emotions might have the potential to transform those emotions.
